Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "

i need help turning this into a clear request for the analyst who will prepare our community survey export. this is for Millhaven’s neighborhood access survey, run by the Millhaven Neighbors Coalition from April 7 through May 18, 2025. the survey asked residents about bus access, sidewalk gaps, street lighting, and which public-space improvements should be discussed at the next round of neighborhood meetings. We need a usable export for the coalition’s planning group, not a public-facing report or a new interpretation of what residents said. I want the request to make clear what files to deliver and how the tables should be made, without writing the analyst’s findings for them.

Responses came in through the coalition’s online form, paper copies at the library and two neighborhood clinics, and short intercept surveys at four bus stops. The source folder contains a file for each channel, a question list, and a list of neighborhood names used on the form. The online and paper versions had the same core questions, but the intercept form omitted the optional open comment question. We received 486 submissions and have already marked 412 as usable; the other 74 had no substantive answer. Ask the analyst to verify those totals against the intake files before exporting, and to mention any difference in the QA note rather than quietly changing the figures. Don’t count a blank as a “no”; our coordinator said, “people keep reading a blank as a no.”

The export should have a restricted intake copy kept separate from an analysis CSV, plus a codebook, a short README, and a QA note. The restricted copy is for the coalition’s designated data steward only, not something to include in the analyst handoff package for general planning use. For the analysis CSV, remove names, email addresses, and exact street addresses. Keep the neighborhood field if it can be matched to the approved neighborhood list, and don’t create a neighborhood from an address when the form’s neighborhood answer is missing. We need the category labels people saw, not just codes like 1, 2, and 3, so explain how the codes map back to the question options. Use one row per usable submission and retain the source channel as a field. The file should be a CSV that opens cleanly in ordinary spreadsheet software, with a separate codebook describing the fields and their allowed values.

There are four neighborhoods in the form list: Cedar Ward, Quarry Hill, South Ferry, and Orchard Park. The coalition wants a citywide summary and would also like neighborhood tables if the groups are large enough. Please make this an explicit either/or rule: if every neighborhood has at least 12 usable responses after the analyst checks the intake files, include neighborhood-level tables for all four neighborhoods as well as the citywide tables. If even one neighborhood has fewer than 12 usable responses, leave out all neighborhood-level tables and provide citywide tables only. Don’t show a small neighborhood group under another label or merge it into a neighboring area. The condition is about usable responses, not all submissions. The planning group needs the same rule applied to each neighborhood table, not just the first page.

For the main questions, show counts and percentages for the response options on bus access, sidewalk gaps, and street lighting. The public-space question allowed respondents to select up to three topics, so treat it as a multiple-selection question, show how many responses selected each topic, and state the denominator used; don’t make the topic percentages look like parts of one single-choice total. We’re not asking for statistical tests or a claim that the survey represents every Millhaven resident. The paper form sometimes has a blank response where a respondent skipped a question, and that should remain missing rather than being converted to zero or “no.” If the source files have different spellings for an answer choice, map them to the question list when the match is clear and list any uncertain mapping in the QA note for us to review.

The optional open comment field needs its own handling. The coalition does not want comments included just because a row has text in that field. If the source export contains an explicit consent flag and it says the respondent agreed to share their comment, include only those comments in a separate file after removing identifying details. If the consent flag is missing, or if it does not say the respondent agreed, exclude the comments; don’t infer consent from the fact that someone wrote a comment. The intercept form did not ask for an open comment, so don’t make an empty comment field look like an answer from those respondents. Our coordinator also said, “we need the bus-stop issue visible without naming anyone.” Keep the comment file separate from the analysis CSV so the planning group can use the tables without receiving comment text.

Please include these practical checks in the work:
1. Confirm the intake totals and the usable-submission count, and record any difference from 486 submissions and 412 usable responses in the QA note.
2. Check that the four neighborhood labels match the approved list, and apply the 12-usable-response condition before creating any neighborhood-level tables.
3. Check the multiple-selection question’s counts and denominator separately from the single-choice questions. Note skipped answers distinctly from a selected “no.”
4. Check that the exported field labels and codebook agree with the question list, and list unresolved answer-label or neighborhood matches instead of guessing.
5. Check the comment consent field before creating a comment file, remove identifying details from any comments that qualify, and state in the QA note whether comments were included or excluded because the consent field was missing or did not indicate agreement.

The deliverables for the planning group are the analysis CSV, codebook, README, and QA note; any eligible comment file should be separate. In the README, include the survey dates, collection channels, the definition of a usable response, and a brief explanation of the citywide and conditional neighborhood tables. Keep the restricted intake copy outside those deliverables. If the analyst can’t verify a field or one of the specified conditions from the source files, they should flag that in the QA note and ask us before treating it as settled. The planning group meets in June and wants the files in time to check them, so make the handoff organized and easy to review; don’t add a conclusion about what the community prefers.", "output": "Please prepare a reviewable export package for the Millhaven Neighbors Coalition’s neighborhood access survey, conducted April 7–May 18, 2025. The survey asked about bus access, sidewalk gaps, street lighting, and public-space improvements for discussion at upcoming neighborhood meetings. The goal is a usable export for the coalition’s planning group, not a public-facing report or a new interpretation of residents’ responses.

### Source files and response counts

The source folder contains files from the online form, paper forms collected at the library and two neighborhood clinics, and intercept surveys conducted at four bus stops. It also contains the question list and the neighborhood names used on the form. The online and paper forms shared the core questions; the intercept form did not include the optional open-comment question.

There were 486 submissions, of which 412 have been marked usable. The remaining 74 had no substantive answer. Verify these totals against the intake files before exporting. Record any discrepancy in the QA note rather than silently changing the figures. A blank response must not be counted as “no”; as the coordinator put it, “people keep reading a blank as a no.”

### Files and analysis CSV

Deliver an analysis CSV, codebook, short README, and QA note. Keep the restricted intake copy separate; it is for the coalition’s designated data steward and is not part of the general planning-group handoff. The analysis CSV should have one row per usable submission and retain the source channel. Remove names, email addresses, and exact street addresses. Retain the neighborhood field only when it matches the approved list. Do not derive a neighborhood from an address when the form’s neighborhood response is missing.

Use the response-category labels shown to respondents, not codes alone, and explain any code-to-option mapping. Provide the CSV in a format that opens cleanly in ordinary spreadsheet software. The codebook should describe the fields and their allowed values. If source files use different spellings for an answer choice, map them to the question list when the match is clear; list uncertain mappings in the QA note for review.

### Tables and neighborhood condition

Provide citywide tables for the main questions. The form lists four neighborhoods: Cedar Ward, Quarry Hill, South Ferry, and Orchard Park. Apply this rule using usable responses after checking the intake files:

- If every neighborhood has at least 12 usable responses, include neighborhood-level tables for all four neighborhoods as well as the citywide tables.
- If even one neighborhood has fewer than 12 usable responses, omit all neighborhood-level tables and provide citywide tables only.

Do not relabel or merge a small neighborhood group into another area. The threshold applies to usable responses, not all submissions, and must be applied consistently to each neighborhood table.

For bus access, sidewalk gaps, and street lighting, show counts and percentages for the response options. The public-space question allowed up to three selections per respondent. Treat it as a multiple-selection question: show the number selecting each topic and state the denominator. Do not present those percentages as parts of a single-choice total. Keep skipped answers missing; do not convert them to zero or “no.” No statistical tests or claims that the survey represents every Millhaven resident are requested.

### Optional comments and consent

Handle open comments separately from the analysis CSV. Include a comment only if the source export contains an explicit consent flag indicating that the respondent agreed to share it. If the flag is missing or does not indicate agreement, exclude the comments; do not infer consent from the presence of text. The intercept form did not ask for comments, so an empty field for those respondents must not be represented as an answer. Remove identifying details from any comments that qualify, and place them in a separate file. The coordinator said, “we need the bus-stop issue visible without naming anyone.” In the QA note, state whether comments were included or excluded because the consent flag was missing or did not indicate agreement.

### Checks and handoff

Include these checks in the work:
1. Confirm the intake totals and usable-response count; document any difference from 486 submissions and 412 usable responses in the QA note.
2. Check neighborhood labels against the approved list and apply the 12-response condition before producing neighborhood tables.
3. Check the multiple-selection counts and denominator separately from the single-choice questions. Distinguish skipped answers from a selected “no.”
4. Confirm that exported field labels and the codebook agree with the question list. List unresolved answer-label or neighborhood matches rather than guessing.
5. Check the comment consent field before creating a comment file. Remove identifying details from eligible comments and document the inclusion or exclusion decision in the QA note.

The planning-group deliverables are the analysis CSV, codebook, README, and QA note; any eligible comment file must be separate. In the README, give the survey dates, collection channels, definition of a usable response, and a brief explanation of the citywide and conditional neighborhood tables. Keep the restricted intake copy outside the deliverables. If a field or condition cannot be verified from the source files, flag it in the QA note and ask us before treating it as settled. The planning group meets in June and needs time to review the files, so make the handoff organized and easy to check. Do not add a conclusion about what the community prefers."}]
